title: Another Week, Another Win For Bullet Brawl's GOAT Nakamura
summary: Like clockwork, GM Hikaru Nakamura won his seventh consecutive Bullet Brawl on Saturday, this time scoring 178 points and finishing ahead of 218 titled players. A 23-game winning streak in the early stages of the arena effectively assured a Nakamura victory. GM Oleksandr Bortnyk finished second with 146 points, edging IM Yoseph Taher by a single point, while IM Aleksandr Usov rounded out the top four with 134 points. Meanwhile, WIM Melika Mohammadi claimed the $100 best women's prize on tiebreaks. The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, October 31, at 12 p.m. ET / 17:00 CET / 9:30 p.m. IST. title: European Chess Club Cup winners crowned in Budva, Montenegro
summary: The 41st European Chess Club Cup and the 30th edition of the European Women’s Chess Club Cup concluded yesterday in Budva, Montenegro. Bayegan Pendik Sports Chess Club (Turkey) emerged as the winner of the Open section, while Cercle d’Échecs de Monte-Carlo successfully defended its title in the Women’s event. The competition took place at the Hotel Slovenska Plaza from October 17 to 23. Both the European Chess Club Cup and the European Women’s Chess Club Cup were 7-round Swiss tournaments. The time control was 90 minutes for 40 moves, plus 30 minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting from move one. With 130 registered teams – 108 in the Open section and 22 in the Women’s section – the event broke the participation record previously set in Rhodes in 2025, where 122 teams competed. Heading into the final round of the Open section, three teams shared the top position: Bayegan Pendik Sports Chess Club (Turkey), SuperChess (Romania), and Novy Bor Chess Club (Czech Republic). The final round featured a top-board clash between Bayegan Pendik and SuperChess, while Novy Bor Chess Club faced Elektroprivreda (Montenegro). After long and intense games, Bayegan Pendik Sports Chess Club prevailed over SuperChess by a narrow score of 3.5–2.5, with victories by GM Anish Giri and GM Amin Tabatabaei against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov and GM Haik Martirosyan, respectively. GM Jorden van Foreest scored for SuperChess after defeating GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, but the other three games were drawn, securing the match win for the Turkish club. Novy Bor Chess Club defeated Elektroprivreda thanks to victories by GMs Nihal Sarin, Pentala Harikrishna, and David Navara, while the other three games were drawn. Scoring 13 match points each, Bayegan Pendik Sports Chess Club and Novy Bor Chess Club tied at the top. However, Bayegan Pendik won on tiebreaks to clinch the title, while Novy Bor Chess Club settled for silver. Rishon LeZion A (Israel) won the bronze medal with 12 match points. Six teams scored 11 match points each, tying for fourth place – a crucial position that guarantees a qualification spot for the inaugural European Super League. Thanks to the best tiebreaks, SuperChess (Romania) finished fourth. Final standings: Open  Ahead of the final round of the Women’s event, three teams were tied for the top: Cercle d’Echecs de Mone-Carlo (Monaco), CE Gambit Bonnevoie (Luxembourg), and Odlar Yurdu (Azerbaijan). Cercle d’Échecs de Monte-Carlo swept the Georgian team to conclude the event with 12 match points. CE Gambit Bonnevoie scored a narrow 2.5–1.5 win over Crvena Zvezda (Serbia) as GM Anna Ushenina and IM Aleksandra Maltsevskaya won their games, while GM Elina Danielian lost to WIM Adela Velikic. The game on board two ended in a draw, bringing CE Gambit Bonnevoie’s final score to 12 match points and a tie for first place. Odlar Yurdu suffered a heavy defeat at the hands of Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica (Serbia) as the Serbian team scored a convincing 3.5–0.5 victory, with their only draw coming on board three. Following the results, Cercle d’Échecs de Monte-Carlo and CE Gambit Bonnevoie tied for first place, but Cercle d’Échecs de Monte-Carlo won on tiebreaks to defend its title and claim the gold medal. Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica and Odlar Yurdu tied for the bronze medal after scoring 10 match points each. With superior tiebreaks, Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica completed the podium. title: Bodhana: youngest female IM ever
summary:
The English Chess Federation hailed her as a ‘generational talent.’ Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, shattered yet another world record, this time becoming the youngest female player in history to qualify for the International Master title. In doing so, she eclipsed a record set 38 years ago by chess great Judit Polgar, widely regarded as the greatest female chess player of all time. | Photo R Oleksiewicz

Bodhana, who is supported by the English Chess Federation, sealed the historic achievement on Friday at the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro, where she was representing the English women's team She Plays To Win Lionesses .

IM Malcolm Pein, the ECF’s Director of International Chess, said: “I can only describe Bodhana as a generational talent. There is no limit to what she can achieve. It’s remarkable that she is more than matching Judit Polgar's achievements at a similar age and breaking her records, even if we live in different times. It's worth noting that Bodhana is the seventh-youngest player, boy or girl, to become an International Master."

True. Here's a list of records:

# Player Age Earned

1 Roman Shogdzhiev (RUS) 10 years, 3 months May 2025

2 Faustino Oro (ARG) 10 years, 8 months, 6 days Jun 2024

3 Abhimanyu Mishra (USA) 10 years, 9 months, 3 days Nov 2019

4 R Praggnanandhaa (IND) 10 years, 9 months, 19 days May 2016

5 Yağız Kaan Erdoğmuş (TUR) 11 years, 1 month, 20 days Jul 2022

6 Javokhir Sindarov (UZB) 11 years, 6 months, 16 days Jun 2017

7 Bodhana Sivanandan (UK) 11 years, 7 months, 16 days October 2026

8 Bharath Subramaniyam (IND) 11 years, 8 months, 8 days Jun 2019

9 Gukesh Dommaraju (IND) 11 years, 9 months, 9 days Mar 2018

10 Sergey Karjakin (UKR) 11 years, 11 months Jan 1990

11 Nodirbek Abdusattorov (UZB) 12 years, 1 day Sep 2016

12 Andy Woodward (USA) 12 years, 1 month, 1 day Jun 2022

Judit Polga r was 12 years and 2 months old when she earned her IM title, in October 1988. That broke the previous record by Bobby Fischer, who was awarded the IM title automatically by FIDE on January 8, 1958, immediately after winning his very first U.S. Chess Championship. His exact age at the conclusion of that tournament was 14 years, 9 months, and 30 days.

An interview after the fifth round of the European Chess Club Cup.

In the interview she says: "If your team wins you get the chance to play even better players. There are so many strong players on board one and both sections. So it's a great experience." Going into the final round she knew she was on the brink of something special. Having already secured two of the three norms required for the IM title, she needed one last result.

ChessBase India video of Bodhana playing her round three game against IM Olga Badelka

Bodhana facing GM Nino Batsiashvili, Georgia , 2459. The game ended in a 85-move draw.

Facing Sweden's Woman International Master Viktoria Johansson, Bodhana completed the task to secure her final norm and qualify for the title. It is another astonishing achievement for the girl, who has been breaking records at a seemingly relentless pace.

History of her rise

Bodhana's extraordinary rise began during the Covid lockdown when, aged five, she discovered a chess set among belongings her father was preparing to throw away. Just a few years later, she was representing England internationally.

In 2024, aged nine, she made her debut at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, becoming the youngest person ever selected to represent England internationally in any sport.

Last year, she became the youngest girl ever to defeat a grandmaster in a classical tournament game – she beat England's GM Peter Wells at the British Chess Championships in Liverpool in 2025 at the age of just 10 years and five months.

This July, she achieved another landmark by defeating French Grandmaster Marc'Andria Maurizzi, rated 2628, at the Dole Open in France, becoming the youngest girl ever to beat a player rated above 2600.

And in August, she was crowned British Women's Chess Champion for the first time after winning a playoff against Woman Grandmaster Trisha Kanyamarala at the British Chess Championships in Coventry.

Bodhana is already Britain's highest-rated female chess player, despite being several years younger than most of her leading rivals.

Now, with the International Master requirements completed before her 12th birthday, the next target is clear: the full grandmaster title, the highest honour in chess.

title: Bayegan Pendik and Monte-Carlo are 2026 European Club Cup champions
summary:
Bayegan Pendik and Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo won the European Club Cup titles in Budva, both finishing level on match points with their closest rivals and prevailing on tiebreaks. Novy Bor took silver in the open section, while Gambit Bonnevoie finished second in the women's competition. Meanwhile, 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan completed her final international master norm, becoming the youngest female player to fulfil the requirements for the title. | Photo: Gerd Densing

Bayegan Pendik, Novy Bor and Rishon LeZion reach the podium

Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club won the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro, after beating defending champions SuperChess Romania 3½–2½ in Friday's final round. The Turkish club finished with 13/14 match points, level with Novy Bor Chess Club, who secured a 4½–1½ victory over Elektroprivreda. Bayegan Pendik claimed the title thanks to their superior tiebreak score. Rishon LeZion A finished third, one match point behind the leading pair.

Three teams entered the seventh round tied for first place, with Bayegan Pendik and SuperChess facing each other in a clash of co-leaders. The Turkish representatives secured the match victory thanks to wins by Anish Giri and Amin Tabatabaei, who defeated Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Haik Martirosyan, respectively. SuperChess collected their only full point through Jorden van Foreest, who beat 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus on board two. The remaining three games ended in draws.

Giri's victory was somewhat surprising, as the Dutch grandmaster had struggled earlier in the event. He had lost two of his previous three games, against Indian grandmasters Pranav Venkatesh and Pranesh M, before facing Abdusattorov, the highest-rated player in the competition. Despite those setbacks, Giri delivered a full point on the top board when his team needed it most.

The crucial SuperChess v. Bayegan Pendik encounter | Photo: Gerd Densing

Meanwhile, Novy Bor defeated Elektroprivreda 4½–1½ to finish level with Bayegan Pendik on match points. The Czech club collected victories on boards two, three and six, with Nihal Sarin beating Karthikeyan Murali, Pentala Harikrishna defeating Velimir Ivic and David Navara overcoming Nikola Djukic.

Novy Bor finished the competition undefeated, with six wins and one draw, the same record as the eventual champions. However, Bayegan Pendik's tiebreak score of 261.5 was 8.5 points higher than Novy Bor's 253.0, leaving the Czech club in second place.

Several Novy Bor players also enjoyed successful individual tournaments. Nihal scored 5/6 and earned the gold medal on board two with a performance rating of 2859. Harikrishna also collected 5/6, taking silver on board three.

Novy Bor, with team captain Petr Boleslav and David Navara holding the Czechian flag during the awards ceremony | Photo: Gerd Densing

The bronze medal went to ninth seeds Rishon LeZion A, who defeated Cheddleton Savills Catering 5½–½ in the final round. The Israeli team, whose squad featured veteran GM and former World Championship challenger Boris Gelfand, finished with 12/14 match points. Their only defeat came against Novy Bor in round four, and they won their remaining six matches.

Cheddleton, seeded 16 th , had entered the final round with a chance to reach the podium after collecting five victories in their first six matches. English international master Richard Pert had contributed six consecutive individual wins to his team's campaign, but suffered his first defeat in the final round. Cheddleton eventually finished twelfth on 10/14 match points.

SuperChess Romania finished fourth with 11/14 match points, ahead of Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai and Alkaloid on tiebreaks. Although they could not defend their European Club Cup title, the Romanian representatives secured a place in the inaugural European Chess Super League, scheduled to take place in 2027.

Rishon LeZion A, the ninth seeds, took home the bronze | Photo: Gerd Densing

The top individual performers on board one: Marc'Andria Maurizzi (Aix-en-Provence), Vaclav Finek (SK Dunajska Streda) and Aydin Suleymanli (Vugar Gashimov) | Photo: Gerd Densing

Women's: Monte-Carlo defend title thanks to 4-0 win

Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo successfully defended their title in the women's European Club Cup, securing a ninth tournament victory after defeating Davit Jojua's Chess Club 4–0 in the final round. The Monaco-based team finished with 12/14 match points, level with CE Gambit Bonnevoie, who defeated Crvena Zvezda 2½–1½. As in the open section, the title was decided by tiebreaks, with Monte-Carlo finishing ahead of the Luxembourg representatives.

Three teams had entered the seventh and final round sharing the lead on 10/12 match points: Monte-Carlo, Gambit Bonnevoie and Odlar Yurdu. The three clubs had already faced each other earlier in the competition, meaning they met lower-ranked opponents on Friday.

Monte-Carlo, the top seeds, faced 15 th seeds Davit Jojua's Chess Club of Georgia. The defending champions secured all four individual points, although Humpy Koneru on board two encountered considerable difficulties against Nia Donghvani before eventually winning her game. Monte-Carlo's convincing result ensured that the team would finish with a strong tiebreak score, regardless of the results of their rivals.

The Monaco-based club suffered their only defeat against Gambit Bonnevoie in round four. Monte-Carlo won their other six matches, concluding the competition with a tiebreak score of 159.5, compared with Gambit Bonnevoie's 145.0.

Elisabeth Paehtz following the games of her teammates Aleksandra Goryachkina and Humpy Koneru | Photo: Gerd Densing

All smiles for the champions - Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo | Photo: Gerd Densing

Gambit Bonnevoie secured their sixth match victory by defeating seventh seeds Crvena Zvezda 2½–1½. Anna Ushenina and Aleksandra Maltsevskaya scored the decisive wins for the Luxembourg team, while Elina Danielian lost to Adela Velikic.

The fourth seeds thus finished second despite having beaten each of the three highest-rated teams in the competition. Gambit Bonnevoie defeated SuperChess Romania in round three, Monte-Carlo in round four and Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica in round five. Their only loss came against Odlar Yurdu in the penultimate round, a result that allowed their closest pursuers to catch them in the standings.

CE Gambit Bonnevoie grabbed silver after recovering from a painful loss in the penultimate round | Photo: Gerd Densing

The bronze medal went to second seeds Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica, who defeated Odlar Yurdu 3½–½. The Serbian team collected three victories and one draw against their Azerbaijani opponents, finishing with 10/14 match points. Odlar Yurdu also finished on 10 points but had to settle for fourth place due to inferior tiebreaks.

Third seeds SuperChess Romania completed the tournament in fifth place with 9/14 match points, followed by Gambit ASEE and Crvena Zvezda on eight points. The top seven seeds eventually occupied the first seven places, although not in their original ranking order.

Bronze goes to Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica | Photo: Gerd Densing

Monte-Carlo also collected three individual gold medals. Aleksandra Goryachkina finished as the best player on board one, Humpy Koneru received gold on board two and Elisabeth Paehtz was the second highest-performing player on board four (which also includes the reserve board). Nurgyul Salimova of Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica took gold on board three.

Still, the most notable achievement of the event came from 11-year-old English star Bodhana Sivanandan, representing She Plays To Win Lionesses A. Sivanandan defeated Sweden's Viktoria Johansson with the black pieces in the final round to complete her third and final international master norm. She finished the tournament with 5½/7 points, comprising five wins, one draw and one defeat.

Having also surpassed the required 2400 rating threshold during the competition, Sivanandan fulfilled the requirements for the IM title at the age of 11 years, 7 months and 16 days. She became the youngest female player to achieve this distinction, surpassing a record held by Judit Polgar since 1988. Formal confirmation remains subject to FIDE's title approval process.

Sivanandan's individual result helped She Plays To Win Lionesses A finish 11 th among the 22 participating teams, one place above their initial seeding. The English squad concluded the competition with 7/14 match points.
